title: Why a nudge is not enough: A social identity critique of governance by stealth
abstract: Abstract Policy makers can use four different modes of governance: ‘hierarchy’, ‘markets’, ‘networks’ and ‘persuasion’. In this article, it is argued that ‘nudging’ represents a distinct (fifth) mode of governance. The effectiveness of nudging as a means of bringing about lasting behaviour change is questioned and it is argued that evidence for its success ignores the facts that many successful nudges are not in fact nudges; that there are instances when nudges backfire; and that there may be ethical concerns associated with nudges. Instead, and in contrast to nudging, behaviour change is more likely to be enduring where it involves social identity change and norm internalisation. The article concludes by urging public policy scholars to engage with the social identity literature on ‘social influence’, and the idea that those promoting lasting behaviour change need to engage with people not as individual cognitive misers, but as members of groups whose norms they internalise and enact.

claims.text: Policy makers can use four different modes of governance: hierarchy, markets, networks, and persuasion.
Nudging represents a distinct, fifth mode of governance.
Nudging is questionable as an effective means of bringing about lasting behaviour change.
Evidence for the success of nudging ignores the fact that many successful nudges are not in fact nudges.
There are instances when nudges backfire.
There may be ethical concerns associated with nudges.
Behaviour change is more likely to be enduring where it involves social identity change and norm internalisation.
Promoting lasting behaviour change requires engaging with people as members of groups whose norms they internalise and enact, rather than as individual cognitive misers.

limitations.text: Existing evidence for nudging success overlooks miscategorization of nudges, backfire instances, and ethical concerns.

future_work.text: Public policy scholars should engage with the social identity literature on social influence to design behavior change interventions based on group norms.

methodologies.name: Social identity critique of nudging
methodologies.description: A theoretical critique applying the social identity literature on social influence to evaluate nudging as a mode of governance.
